segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back the four winds of the earth, so that no wind would blow on the earth or on the sea or on any tree.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw another angel coming up from the rising of the sun, holding the seal of the living God, and he cried out with a loud voice to the four angels who had been permitted to harm the earth and the sea,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees until we have sealed the slaves of our God on their foreheads.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I heard the number of those who were sealed, a hundred and forty-four thousand, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: from the tribe of Judah, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Reuben, twelve thousand; from the tribe of Gad, twelve thousand;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: from the tribe of Asher, twelve thousand; from the tribe of Naphtali, twelve thousand; from the tribe of Manasseh, twelve thousand;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: from the tribe of Simeon, twelve thousand; from the tribe of Levi, twelve thousand; from the tribe of Issachar, twelve thousand;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: from the tribe of Zebulun, twelve thousand; from the tribe of Joseph, twelve thousand; from the tribe of Benjamin, twelve thousand sealed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After these things I looked, and there was a great crowd that no one could count, from every nation and from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they cry out with a loud voice, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Salvation belongs to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And all the angels were standing around the throne and the elders and the four living creatures, and they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might belong to our God forever and ever. Amen.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then one of the elders spoke up and said to me,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “These who are clothed in the white robes, who are they, and where have they come from?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “My lord, you know.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to me,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “These are the ones coming out of the great affliction; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For this reason they are before the throne of God, and they serve him day and night in his temple, and the one who sits on the throne will spread his tent over them.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: They will hunger no more and thirst no more; the sun will never beat down on them, nor any scorching heat,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: because the Lamb at the center of the throne will shepherd them and guide them to springs of the waters of life, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.”

notes.phrase: the seal of the living God
notes.traditional: the seal of the living God
notes.note: A seal was a signet, usually a ring or engraved stone, pressed into wax or clay to mark ownership and guarantee protection. Marking the forehead recalls Ezekiel 9, where those who are marked are spared when judgment falls on Jerusalem. The sealing here marks people as God's property; it does not necessarily promise exemption from suffering.

The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and the seal on the forehead fits that picture of ownership. Most English versions use “servants,” partly because in the Greek Old Testament “slave of God” was an honorable title for Moses, David and the prophets. Both associations would have been heard by a first-century reader; “slaves” is kept here because “servant” now suggests a paid employee free to leave.

The number is twelve times twelve times a thousand, and most interpreters take it as symbolic of completeness. Whether this group is the same as the uncountable crowd of verse 9 is disputed. On one view John hears the number and then sees the crowd, two pictures of one people. On the other, the 144,000 are a distinct group, such as Jewish believers. The Greek does not settle it.

This list matches no Old Testament list of the tribes. Judah, the tribe of the Messiah, comes first instead of the firstborn Reuben. Dan is missing, and both Joseph and his son Manasseh are counted while Ephraim is not named. The reasons for the omission of Dan are debated; an association of that tribe with idolatry is the explanation most often proposed.

The Greek word here is the same one that in the plural is often translated “Gentiles,” meaning the non-Jewish peoples. In Revelation, where the scope is all the peoples of the world, it is rendered “nation” or “nations.”

Palm branches were carried in celebrations of victory and at festivals, especially the Feast of Tabernacles, and the crowd waves them when Jesus enters Jerusalem in John 12:13. Together with the white robes they mark the scene as a victory celebration.

The Greek is a shout without a verb: “The salvation to our God.” In the Greek Old Testament the word often means deliverance or victory won in battle, and some translators render it “Victory” here. The traditional “salvation” is kept, but the sense is that the rescue is God's achievement and the credit is his.

The word means pressure, distress or oppression and is the ordinary term for the sufferings of God's people; “the great affliction” echoes Daniel 12:1. “Tribulation” has become a technical term in some modern end-time schemes, which a first-century reader would not have heard in it. Whether a single final crisis or the whole course of persecution is meant is disputed.

notes.traditional: they which came out / the ones who have come out
notes.note: The Greek uses a present participle, which may picture people still arriving as John watches. It may equally be a timeless description, “those who come out,” and many versions translate it as a completed action. The rendering here keeps the present form.

notes.phrase: will spread his tent over them
notes.note: The verb means to pitch a tent or encamp, and with the preposition “over” it pictures God's tent stretched above the worshippers as shelter. It recalls the tabernacle, the tent of God's presence in the wilderness. Many versions paraphrase as “dwell among them” or “shelter them with his presence.”

notes.phrase: They will hunger no more and thirst no more
notes.traditional: They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more
notes.note: Verses 16 and 17 weave together promises from Isaiah without quoting them formally. No hunger, thirst or scorching sun, and guidance to springs of water, come from Isaiah 49:10; God wiping away tears comes from Isaiah 25:8. In Isaiah it is God who shepherds and guides; here that role is given to the Lamb.

candidates.reason: Occurs throughout the New Testament, and the choice between “slave” and “servant” changes how readers hear both parables and titles like “slave of God,” so it should be fixed once.
Translators vary between tribulation, affliction, distress, trouble and suffering across the Gospels, Paul and Revelation, and “tribulation” carries modern end-time baggage.
It denotes cultic service to a deity and is rendered “serve” or “worship” inconsistently, which blurs it with προσκυνέω.
It ranges from bowing in homage to a superior to worship of God, and a consistent policy is needed for the Gospels and Revelation alike.
It names the sanctuary proper as distinct from ἱερόν, the whole temple complex, and English “temple” for both hides a distinction that matters in several books.
